classification.difficultyReason: Requires translating verbal minimum and total constraints into inequalities, graphing their common region, and interpreting bar counts as integer points to list all feasible combinations.

inlines.text: Benji wants to buy some chocolate bars. He decides to buy
He wants at least two caramel bars.
He wants at least one wafer bar.
His mum says he can have no more than 5 bars altogether.
Illustrate the problem above using inequalities on a graph and list the different ways he can buy the chocolate bars.

answer.short: $x\ge1$, $y\ge2$, $x+y\le5$, with $x,y$ integers. The possible numbers of (wafer, caramel) bars are $(1,2)$, $(1,3)$, $(1,4)$, $(2,2)$, $(2,3)$ and $(3,2)$. The acceptable region is the unshaded triangle, including its boundaries.
answer.worked:
At least one wafer bar gives $x\ge1$; at least two caramel bars gives $y\ge2$; no more than five bars altogether gives $x+y\le5$.

Draw solid boundaries $x=1$, $y=2$ and $y=5-x$. The last line has intercepts $(0,5)$ and $(5,0)$. Shade the unwanted regions $x<1$, $y<2$ and $y>5-x$. The unshaded triangle has vertices $(1,2)$, $(1,4)$ and $(3,2)$, and all three boundaries are included.

The numbers of bars must be integers. Reading the integer points in the acceptable region gives:

- 1 wafer, 2 caramel
- 1 wafer, 3 caramel
- 1 wafer, 4 caramel
- 2 wafer, 2 caramel
- 2 wafer, 3 caramel
- 3 wafer, 2 caramel

spec.description: Coordinate graph with unwanted regions shaded blue and the acceptable closed triangular region unshaded. Horizontal ticks run from −2 to 5 and vertical ticks from −1 to 5.
spec.mathematics: x >= 1, y >= 2, x + y <= 5. Solid boundaries x = 1, y = 2 and y = 5 - x. Acceptable triangle vertices (1,2), (1,4), (3,2).
